title: Cluster & Pod Security
intro: RBAC controls who can talk to the API server, but that's only half of cluster security — SecurityContext and Pod Security Standards control what a container is allowed to do once it's actually running.

steps.prompt: Check the 'web' pod's security context to see what privileges its container actually runs with.
steps.explanation: This container runs as a non-root user with a read-only root filesystem and can't escalate privileges — a compromised process inside it has meaningfully less it can do to the host.
steps.why: Without an explicit securityContext, many container images default to running as root — jsonpath is the fast way to confirm a pod actually has these hardening settings instead of trusting the deployment author remembered to add them.

steps.prompt: Check which Pod Security Standard level is enforced on this namespace.
steps.explanation: Pod Security Admission reads these labels directly off the namespace — 'restricted' is the strictest built-in level, blocking things like privileged containers and host networking at admission time, before a pod is even created.
steps.why: This replaced the older PodSecurityPolicy (removed in newer Kubernetes versions) — the whole policy now lives as three namespace labels (enforce/audit/warn) instead of a separate cluster-wide resource.

steps.prompt: A teammate's new pod manifest got rejected. Try creating a privileged pod in this namespace to see the actual admission error yourself.
steps.fake_output: Error from server (Forbidden): pods "bad-pod" is forbidden: violates PodSecurity "restricted:latest": privileged (container "bad-pod" must not set securityContext.privileged=true)
steps.explanation: This is rejected before the pod object is even created — Pod Security Admission runs at admission time, not as a runtime check afterward.
steps.why: Compare this to a NetworkPolicy or RBAC rule, which only take effect once something is already running — Pod Security Admission is a hard gate at creation time, which is exactly why it's the right tool for 'never allow privileged containers here' rather than catching it after the fact.

steps.prompt: Check whether the 'ci-bot' ServiceAccount from earlier could delete secrets in this namespace — a real security review question, not just a curiosity.
steps.explanation: Confirming the negative matters as much as confirming the positive — this is exactly the kind of check a security review or audit would run against every service account with any elevated access.
steps.why: Same 'auth can-i --as=' pattern from the RBAC tutorial — the difference here is the intent: you're not debugging a broken permission, you're proactively verifying a boundary holds before it's ever tested by an actual incident.
